# The Assignment I’m Not Dropping

Jess texted me last night: “It’s one assignment. Don’t torch your job over it.”

I know what she meant. She wasn’t telling me to stop caring. She was reminding me that caring doesn’t make the consequences disappear. Half the group chat agreed with her, which is fair. I could spend the next fifteen texts explaining myself, but I’d rather try to say it properly once.

I’m not mad at Jess. We met student teaching in 2012, at the same school, when we were both trying to figure out how to teach a room full of teenagers without looking like we were trying to figure out how to teach a room full of teenagers. She left teaching in 2019 and now works in HR at a biotech in Cambridge. She knows what it’s like to be responsible for a room of kids. She also knows you can’t pay rent with the satisfaction of having made a principled point.

And she’s right: I could get burned. I’m tenured—I’ve been since 2021—but Dr. Halvorsen still controls my schedule and who gets AP. Tenure doesn’t mean there’s no price for being difficult. I’m scared, a little. I’m not brave about this.

Here’s what the assignment is. I teach two sections of US History II to juniors at Cobb Street High. For the last four years, I’ve asked students to interview someone in their family or neighborhood about Boston’s busing and desegregation crisis in 1974–76. They make a ten-minute recording and write a two-page reflection. In four years, this is the first complaint.

It came by email to Dr. Halvorsen, with a school committee member copied. The parent said the project “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.” On Thursday, November 19, at 3:15, I’m meeting with Dr. Halvorsen and the parent.

I don’t think she’s making this up. The project can bring up painful things. And asking a kid to interview family can put them in a tough spot, especially if they don’t know what they’ll hear, or don’t feel free to decline. That’s a real problem with the assignment, not a made-up objection I can brush off because I like the project.

So I’m changing it. Students will still be able to interview someone in their family or neighborhood, but there will be another option: interview a librarian or archivist, or use recorded interviews from past years—with permission. No kid has to interview family.

That’s the line for me: I don’t get to force anyone. But I also don’t want discomfort, by itself, to be a reason we never look closely at the past.

In 2023, a student I’ll call D. interviewed his grandmother. She’d driven a school bus in Southie in 1974. She had never told anyone in the family about it. D. played about forty seconds of the recording for the class. Then nobody said a word for what felt like a full minute.

I don’t mean that as a tidy story where one assignment heals everything. It didn’t. It was forty seconds of one woman’s life, and then a quiet classroom. But her story had been there all along, just outside the version of history most of us had heard.

Last year, one girl found out her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was upset. We talked after class twice. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year—not because it arrived at the right answer, or because she made a lesson out of it. It was thoughtful because she tried to make room for something she hadn’t known and didn’t want to be true.

I don’t want every student to have an experience like that. I don’t want to turn someone’s family history into an assignment they can’t safely say no to. That’s why I’m adding the alternative. But these are the kids who live in this city, and this is the history of the place they live. The textbook gives it one paragraph.

Jess, I get why you said not to torch my job over one assignment. I also get that from outside the classroom, this may look like a lot of risk for a ten-minute recording and two pages. Maybe it is. I’m not asking you to agree that the project is worth the trouble. I want you to understand why I’m not ready to drop it quietly.

The meeting is Thursday. I’m going to listen, explain what I’m changing, and try not to turn it into a fight with the parent. I’m not looking for one. I think she has a point about pressure, and I want the assignment to do better by the kids who might feel it most.

Then I’ll text you afterward. I’ll probably have a lot to say, so you can decide whether you want the short version or the full group-chat-length one.
